title: Bitcoin back down to 60k - does crypto have real value?
subtitle: Supply and demand, macro, the network effect and market sentiment
openingQuestion: Which factor do supporters usually use to explain Bitcoin's value?
openingOptions: Fixed supply and the network effect
The accounting profit the network generates
explanation: Bitcoin does not rest on conventional cash flow; it is usually seen through scarcity, the network effect and market belief. Because there is no discounted-cash-flow valuation model for it the way there is for a share, the range its price swings through is normally far wider than that of a traditional asset, and the price can move a long way on a change of sentiment alone.

realWorldExample.description: Digital assets swing hard because their valuation depends heavily on expectations, liquidity and market sentiment.

quiz.question: What makes Bitcoin different from a traditional share?
options: It has no underlying cash flow
It has no real users at all
It cannot be traded on an exchange
It has no price movement at all
quiz.explanation: Valuing crypto generally does not follow the framework of a business generating cash flow the way a share does. The other three options are simply not true of Bitcoin: it has a large user base, it trades on exchanges around the clock, and its price is famously among the most volatile of any traded asset.

quiz.question: Why do traditional valuation models like DCF or P/E not work for Bitcoin?
options: Because Bitcoin is too new to have enough history to compute with
Because the law forbids using DCF to value digital assets
Because Bitcoin has no cash flow or profit to discount
Because Bitcoin always rises, so there is no point valuing it
quiz.explanation: DCF discounts the future cash flow of a business; P/E compares profit against the share price - both need a 'business' producing profit or cash. Bitcoin is not a business and produces no cash flow, so its value rests entirely on supply and demand, belief and the network effect rather than on traditional cash-flow models. Its age is not the obstacle: a fifteen-year history would be plenty if there were a cash flow to discount.

quiz.question: Why can DCF not be used to value Bitcoin the way it values a business?
options: Because Bitcoin has no value at all in the real economy
Because Bitcoin's cash flow is too large for the model to handle
Because DCF only works for companies listed on an exchange
Because Bitcoin produces no cash flow to discount
quiz.explanation: DCF needs a future cash flow to discount. Bitcoin does not produce cash flow in that sense, so a cash-flow-based valuation tool simply does not apply - not because the tool is wrong. DCF is used on unlisted companies all the time, so listing is not the issue either.

quiz.question: Which other asset also produces no cash flow yet has long been recognised by the market as having value, on similar logic to Bitcoin?
options: Gold (a precious metal)
Shares in a growth company
Rental property
Government bonds
quiz.explanation: Gold is valued through scarcity and its role as a store of value rather than through cash flow, the classic example that an asset can have real value without a discounted-cash-flow model. The other three all produce cash: growth shares have earnings, rental property has rent, and a bond pays a coupon.

quiz.question: Bitcoin has no cash flow, so it cannot be valued by discounting. What approach is usually used instead?
options: Working out the network's book value from the electricity cost already spent on mining
Comparing it with other scarce assets and estimating the market it could take
Using the profit multiples of the largest cryptocurrency exchanges
Discounting the transaction fees the network collects to present value
quiz.explanation: With no cash flow there is no intrinsic value in the classical sense, so the common approach is to estimate the share of a market it could displace - gold, safe-haven assets - and divide by the supply. That is a reference frame, not a valuation. Mining cost is a cost, not a value; and the exchanges are businesses whose profits say nothing about the asset itself.

keyTakeaways: Crypto is usually seen through supply, the network effect and sentiment
Valuing it is nothing like valuing a share
Volatility and liquidity are the things to manage

practicePrompt.question: When Bitcoin corrected from 73k to 60k USD, what factors does the macro financial lens use to explain that move?
options: Macro liquidity, ETFs, risk appetite
Because the Bitcoin source code expired
Because governments banned the use of the Internet
Because Bitcoin has no buying or selling at all
practicePrompt.explanation: The crypto price is heavily affected by global macro liquidity, the buying and selling flows of institutional ETFs, and the market's risk appetite.

summary.keyIdea: Crypto is usually seen through supply, the network effect and sentiment
summary.commonMistake: Easy to miss: valuing it is nothing like valuing a share
summary.action: Volatility and liquidity are the things to manage

application.secondary: Getting this principle solid lifts your professional financial analysis.

sections.text: Bitcoin and other digital assets cannot be valued with DCF or P/E - not because those tools are poor, but because what Bitcoin is differs completely from a business.
Why traditional valuation models do not apply

DCF discounts the future cash flow of a business; P/E compares profit against the share price - both need a 'business' producing profit or cash flow. Bitcoin is not a business and produces no cash flow, so its value depends entirely on fixed scarce supply, the network effect (value rising as more people use it), and market belief - not on traditional cash-flow models.

items: Bitcoin has no underlying cash flow, so DCF and P/E do not apply
Value rests on scarcity (fixed supply), the network effect and market belief
Lacking a traditional valuation anchor, the price swings far more than an asset with cash flow

sections.title: Three valuation factors standing in for cash flow

concepts.def: Total Bitcoin supply is capped by the protocol and cannot be issued at will the way fiat money can - the same scarcity logic as gold.
The network's value rises as more people use it, more places accept payment in it, and more infrastructure is built around it.
With no cash flow anchoring the value, sentiment and market narrative move the price far more than they do for an asset with cash flow.

left.label: Company shares
left.text: There is cash flow, profit and assets - things that can be discounted to present value with DCF or compared with P/E. The value has an anchor, imperfect as it is.

right.label: Bitcoin
right.text: No cash flow is produced and there is no 'profit' to compare. Value rests entirely on supply and demand, belief and network utility - with no traditional anchor, so the range of movement is far wider.

sections.label: This does not mean 'no value'
sections.text: Plenty of assets that produce no cash flow still have real value - gold is the classic example, valued through scarcity and its role as a store of value across thousands of years without any DCF model. Many people see Bitcoin through the same logic, but with a far shorter history, so the uncertainty about its long-term value is far greater too.

lines: That DCF does not apply does not mean Bitcoin has no value.
It only means it needs a different frame to assess, not the frame of a business.
